**Small Thunder**

The last mechanical cash register in the city rang for the final time on a Tuesday in March, and Nora was there to record it.

Mr. Alvi had run the hardware store for forty-one years. His last sale was a box of finishing nails, seventy-nine cents, marked down from a price he'd written by hand. He slid them across the counter and looked at the register the way you look at a horse you've decided not to sell after all. "Go on," he told her. "Do it again."

She didn't need asking twice. The drawer sprang with a sound like a bell struck inside a wooden box — the ka-ching everyone thinks they remember from old movies, except realer, thicker, with a rattle in the tail where the drawer bounced on its runners. She recorded it four more times. On the fifth, Mr. Alvi laid his hand flat on the brass top, and she caught the small stunned silence of that too.

This is her job, more or less. Nora archives vanishing sounds. Not the big ones — symphonies, speeches; others have those covered. The small ones. The coin return of the last payphone, which still advertised a pizza parlor in grease pencil. The dial-up modem's shriek, which she once described to a twelve-year-old as the sound of the internet clearing its throat. The clunk-and-roll of a vending machine delivering a can of root beer.

She has rules. She records in the wild when she can, because a typewriter is only a typewriter if someone is typing. She logs date, location, temperature — cold changes pitch — because sound is just air remembering what happened to it, and air cares about the weather.

The project started in her mother's kitchen. Or ended there — she's never sure which. Her mother was dying the way a house is demolished: slowly, then all at once. One afternoon she stood in that kitchen, heard the pressure cooker begin its hiss, and thought, absurdly: who will know what this sounded like? So she held up her phone. She got the cooker, the drawer with the loose runner, the faucet that needed a quarter-turn past sensible. The screen door took two tries, because the door was really two sounds — the slam, then the latch catching half a second later, like an echo with a job. And underneath it all, her mother humming in the next room. A song Nora still can't name.

Her mother died that October. Nora has forty-seven minutes of a kitchen. She has never played a second of it.

People find her. Mostly they want things she can get: church bells, milk bottles, a rotary phone dialed with a pencil. But last winter a man named Frank wrote about his wife's sewing machine. A treadle-powered Singer, 1919. He didn't want the machine, he said. He wanted *her* using it — the rhythm, the way she slowed at the ends of seams, the way when she stopped, the treadle did a little dying fall, "like a music box giving up." He'd tried humming it to his granddaughter; it came out wrong. He closed politely: *I know this isn't something you can record.*

He was right, and she tried anyway. She found a working Singer at an estate sale, oiled it, set a microphone by the treadle. It ran beautifully. It sounded like nothing. The mechanism was perfect, but the rhythm — the hesitations, the speed of a woman deciding — was gone, because it had never lived in the machine. It lived in Lorraine's foot. (Frank mentioned her name once, casually, the way you mention someone still in the room.) She recorded the empty machine anyway and sent it with a note about what was missing.

Frank wrote back the next morning. *That's not it,* he said. *But thank you. It's close enough to miss her by.*

She has that sentence pinned above her desk. The truest thing anyone has said about her profession. Every archive is a bet that the copy will carry some of the original, and every archivist knows it won't. You keep the jar, not the summer. You do it anyway.

Lately she's started recording things that aren't vanishing yet: her refrigerator at 3 a.m., the crowd at a little-league game, rain on her particular roof, which is not the same as rain on yours. A new phase of the project, or the end of her objectivity — she's decided it doesn't matter. Everything is the last of its kind if you wait long enough. The trick isn't catching things before they go. It's noticing they're here.

In September she drove out to a farm to record a woman canning tomatoes: lids into the kettle, tongs, the thick plop of fruit packed in glass. Then, as the kitchen cooled, the jars began to seal themselves one by one. Ping. Pause. Ping. Each lid sucking down tight, locking in August as well as it could.

The woman caught her expression. "My mother called that small thunder," she said.

Nora kept recording and thought: this is the whole archive. The entire impossible job. Not the keeping — the sound the keeping makes. Ping. Pause. Ping. Not lost; sealed.

Somewhere in her desk, a kitchen waits in the dark with its hand on the lid. Forty-seven minutes. The slam, the latch catching half a second behind, the humming underneath it all. She'll play it someday. Not yet. Some jars take years to cool, and you have to be standing in the kitchen to hear the thunder.

The last mechanical cash register in the city rang for the final time on a Tuesday in March, and Nora was there to record it.

The screen door took two tries, because the door was really two sounds — the slam, then the latch catching half a second later, like an echo with a job. Underneath it all, faintly, her mother humming from the next room. A song Nora still can't name.

He wanted her using it — the rhythm, the way she slowed at the ends of seams, the way when she stopped, the treadle did a little dying fall, "like a music box giving up." Nora kept the recorder running and thought: this is the whole archive. The entire impossible job. Not the keeping — the sound the keeping makes. Ping. Pause. Ping. Not lost; sealed.

Somewhere in her desk, a kitchen waits in the dark with its hand on the lid. Forty-seven minutes. The slam, the latch catching half a second behind, the humming underneath it all.
